title: Cartesian products and real intervals
section: Set Theory ▷ Cartesian Products; Intervals of the Real Line
terms: Cartesian product; ordered pair; open interval; closed interval; half-open interval; un- bounded interval; extended real numbers.

exposition.text:
The Cartesian product A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} records ordered pairs. For finite sets,
|A × B| = |A||B|; if either factor is empty, the product is empty. An interval in R contains every
real number between any two of its points. Parentheses exclude finite endpoints and brackets
include them.
The extended real line adjoins −∞, +∞ for bounds and limits; in ordinary real intervals these
are not included endpoints. Coordinate conditions describe products exactly, so boundary mem-
bership requires checking each coordinate. Infinite unions and intersections of intervals demand
attention to whether an endpoint ever occurs or survives every set.
Explicitly, (a, b) = {x : a < x < b}, [a, b] = {x : a ≤ x ≤ b}, and [a, b) or (a, b] includes exactly
the indicated endpoint. In R, [a, ∞) is unbounded but has only real elements. In the extended
real line, an interval such as [a, +∞] can instead include the adjoined element +∞; the ambient
space must be stated.

solution.text:
Both 0 and 1 lie in every interval, as does every point between them. If x < 0 or x > 1,
choose n sufficiently large that the corresponding endpoint passes x, excluding it. Thus the
intersection is [0, 1].

Intersection of products is (A ∩ B)×(B ∩ C). Here A∩ B = [1, 2] and B ∩C = [2, 3), yielding
the stated rectangle.

solution.text:
Neither endpoint zero nor one is in any interval. Every point strictly between them lies in
one for all sufficiently large n, so the union is (0, 1).

Let I = [n, ∞) as subsets of R, and J = [n, +∞] as subsets of the extended real line.
n=1 n=1
Which pair (I, J) is correct?
(A) (∅, ∅) (B) ({+∞}, {+∞}) (C) (∅, {+∞}) (D) (R, {+∞}) (E) (∅, [−∞, +∞])

solution.text:
Every finite real x is smaller than some positive integer n, so no real point survives all the
intervals. In the extended line, +∞ is explicitly included by the bracket in every interval
for J. It is not an element of the ordinary real intervals defining I.

question.text:
For arbitrary sets A, B, which condition is equivalent to A × B = B × A?
(A) A = B
(B) A ⊆ B
(C) A ∩ B ̸= ∅
(D) A = B or at least one of A, B is empty
(E) |A| = |B|

solution.text:
If either set is empty, both products are empty. If both are nonempty, fix an element of
each. For any a ∈ A, pairing it with a fixed b ∈ B and using equality shows a ∈ B; revers-
ing the argument gives B ⊆ A. Hence A = B. Equal cardinality alone does not identify
coordinate sets.
